name: Organic silicium mesotherapy

lead: Organic silicium is a silicon-containing preparation that some mesotherapy practitioners add to injected cocktails. Mesotherapy delivers small amounts of ingredients into or just under the skin, and silicium is included in mixes aimed at skin quality, hair and localised fat.

The one trial in the research record is a 2007 pilot of 12 patients with submental (under-chin) fat comparing phosphatidylcholine alone with phosphatidylcholine plus organic silicium. Hair-specific trials of silicium mesotherapy have not been identified.

paras: In clinics the cocktail is injected in a series of sessions about two weeks apart, as in the pilot study.[1] Combination with other ingredients is typical of mesotherapy generally.

Mesotherapy mixes are practitioner-compounded and not FDA-approved. The American Society for Dermatologic Surgery said in 2005 further study was warranted, the American Society of Plastic Surgeons did not endorse mesotherapy, and several South American countries ban it.[2] Adverse events attributed to unhygienic conditions led to a short-lived French ban in 2011.[2]

angle.text: Practitioners include silicium in mixes for skin quality, hair and local fat deposits. The research available is a small pilot on under-chin fat.

lead: Organic silicium mesotherapy refers to injecting an organic silicon compound as part of a mesotherapy mixture, a practice that spread through cosmetic and hair-restoration clinics, where silicon is also marketed for skin firmness.

Mesotherapy itself was developed by French physician Michel Pistor, the term was coined by French press in 1958, and the French Academy of Medicine recognised it as a specialty in 1987.[1] It involves intradermal or subcutaneous injection of pharmaceuticals, plant extracts, vitamins or other substances.[1]

The only trial found compared phosphatidylcholine alone against phosphatidylcholine plus organic silicium for submental fat in 12 patients over one to five sessions about two weeks apart, measuring fat with a caliper and digital photography.[2]
infobox: Practitioner mixes fall under state medical boards[1]

paras: Mesotherapy uses small injections of mixtures into the skin or fat layer, with the stated aims of nourishing and rejuvenating skin and acting on fat cells.[1] Organic silicium is one ingredient used in such mixes; a 1981 French paper also used an organic silicium cream as a diagnostic aid for sweat-pore counting.[3]

A 2007 pilot study in 12 patients with submental fat deposits compared injections of phosphatidylcholine alone with phosphatidylcholine plus organic silicium. Patients received one to five sessions about two weeks apart, and fat was measured with a vernier caliper and digital photography.[2] No studies of silicium mesotherapy specifically for hair were found. Reviews of mesotherapy in general describe cosmetic uses as not tested in standard clinical trials.[1]

The FDA does not regulate practitioners who inject mixtures; this falls to state medical boards.[1] The American Society for Dermatologic Surgery said in 2005 that further study was warranted.[1] Brazil and several South American countries ban it.[1] France banned it for fat removal in April 2011 but the Council of State cancelled the ban that June.[1]
